overview.what: A Redis cache is placed in front of session token verification. The public contract of TokenService.verify() is unchanged: same signature, same exceptions, same ordering of checks.
overview.why: Every authenticated request currently makes a Postgres round trip to re-validate a token that was verified milliseconds earlier. At the morning peak this accounts for 40% of queries hitting the database.
overview.mental_model:
A request's token still goes through the same two checks: its signature is decoded first, then its session is confirmed as still active. Only the second check changes. It now asks the cache first and only falls back to the database on a miss, writing the answer back so the next request finds it.

Revocation is the other half of the change. Revoking a session now removes its cache entry as well as its database row, so a revoked token cannot keep passing the second check through a stale entry.

decisions.choice: The cache is described by a three-method Protocol rather than an abstract base class.
decisions.reason: Tests can pass a plain dict without inheriting anything, and Redis stays a dependency of the infrastructure layer only.

decisions.choice: Revocation deletes the cache entry immediately instead of relying on a short cache lifetime.
decisions.reason: A short lifetime only narrows the window in which a revoked token still works, and a revocation needs that window closed.

overview.risks: A revoked token left in the cache would be accepted as valid. Step 4 handles this; it is the step that deserves the most attention.

steps.title: A contract before an implementation
steps.narrative: Before writing anything Redis-specific, this step pins down the minimal contract the auth service needs from a cache: read a value, write it with a lifetime, delete it. Everything else Redis offers (pipelines, scans, stats) is deliberately left out, so the service cannot come to depend on it.

files.why: A Protocol rather than an abstract base class: tests can pass a plain dict without inheriting anything, and Redis stays a dependency of the infrastructure layer only.

steps.title: Wiring the cache in without changing the public contract
steps.narrative:
The cache slots into verify() without changing anything a caller can observe: the signature, the exceptions and the order of the checks are all identical.

The service receives the cache from the dependency container instead of building it itself. That is what lets the tests pass a fake, and it also means every request shares one cache instance, and therefore one Redis connection pool, rather than opening a connection each time.

files.why: The cache read happens after signature decoding, not before. A badly signed token must never be used as a lookup key, otherwise the signature stops protecting anything.

watchpoints.note: Cache-unavailable path falls back to the database — confirm this against step 5.

hunks.note: The write-back uses the row's remaining TTL, not a fixed one, so the cache entry can never outlive the session.

steps.title: Invalidation on revocation
steps.narrative:
This is the step to read most carefully. Without it, revoking a session would leave its token valid until the cache entry expired on its own.

The entry is therefore deleted as part of the revocation itself, in the same logical operation as the database update. If Redis is unreachable, the whole revocation fails and the caller sees an error, rather than the token quietly staying cached.

files.why: The cache delete runs in the same logical transaction as the database revocation and before returning to the caller: if Redis fails, the revocation fails too and surfaces as an error.

watchpoints.note: Ordering is deliberate — database first, cache second. Reversed, a crash between the two would leave a revoked token valid.
Bulk revocation loops over jtis; acceptable up to a few dozen sessions, a real risk beyond that.

files.why: drop() completes the contract. A missing key is not an error: revoking a token that was never cached is a normal case.
